utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're going to deal with these statements, so I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first thing we need to do is to decide on a procedure. Your intention, as I understand it, was to call these witnesses in the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're faced with some logistical problems, and in order to ensure that we were able to fill the Court's schedule for the remaining weeks, I had asked that the decision on these nine witnesses be expedited. Some of the logistical problems have been solved. There still may be the possibility of smaller gaps, but it is not as urgent as I first believed last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we heard the argument now and gave a decision next Tuesday, is that going to present any problems to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That's what we'll do. We've got the nine witnesses we have to deal with. And taking them in the order which you set out in your annex, there are five for which you concede that cross-examination is appropriate, beginning with 1750. There's no concession there. This is -- deals with deportation and forced labour and destruction of cultural property in Bijeljina. Yes. Is there anything you want to say about that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I would just note that upon further reflection and another reading of the statements, there are really only two witnesses who the Prosecution would be proposing that they should be -- their evidence should be taken without cross-examination. B1750, as well as a number of other witnesses, or most of the other witnesses, the Prosecution would concede that a -- a live issue is raised and that it would be appropriate for the witnesses to be called for cross-examination. The only exception to those seven witnesses would be Witness 1488. That witness the Prosecution would also concede that under the Appeals Chamber's analysis in Galic, that that witness probably also speaks to some evidence that would be considered proximate to the accused, and in the case of that witness, the Prosecution would be requesting that the statement be accepted under 92 bis and that the Prosecution only lead that portion of the evidence which would be considered proximate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So 1488 you would be calling some evidence live.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what's the position about 1750?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The position of the Prosecution, Your Honour, is that it is not proximate to the acts and conduct of the accused. The amici, through Mr. Kay, have agreed to that, or put the same position forward. The Prosecution does concede that a live -- a substantive reference to the JNA is made in that statement and it is appropriate that the witness be called for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. 1524 seems to be the next on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is one of the witnesses that the Prosecution submits that -- I'm sorry, I withdraw that. That is one of the witnesses who I had originally submitted cross-examination was not necessary in the 92 bis, but upon a more careful reading of the statement and further analysis about the importance of the evidence to the entire case, I would concede that that -- cross-examination is appropriate in that -- in the case of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. 1460, you've conceded some cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I would note that the Prosecution's position, and in concurrence with the amici's position, is that it's not proximate to the acts and conduct of the accused. It is cumulative of two witnesses that have testified, B-1455 and B-1146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. 1516?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is one of the witnesses who the Prosecution submits that cross-examination is not necessary. This witness's testimony is -- or evidence is cumulative of the testimony of B-1416. It does not go to the acts or conduct of the accused. There is no reference to the JNA but for the presence of a JNA sitting on a bridge in March of 1992. It is the Prosecution's position that this is such a de minimis reference to the JNA that even though it is a reference, it does not raise a live issue in the case, and therefore cross-examination is not warranted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1097 and 1704, both of them you've conceded cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Anything to add about them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is the other witness who the Prosecution submits cross-examination is not warranted. This witness was cumulative of B-1701. If the Chamber recall, 1701 testified about events in Bratunac, and there was extensive cross-examination regarding whether the people who the witness claimed or said were in JNA uniforms were in fact really JNA. The accused had a full opportunity to cross-examine him on that. This witness's testimony is essentially the same, except that this witness says that though the -- although the people were in JNA uniforms, he did not believe that they were active JNA members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But he described some of them, I think, as local Serbs, at one stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. So it does not appear that producing this witness for cross-examination will -- The statement taken at face value suggests what the -- the point that the accused made with B-1701. The Prosecution will be introducing other evidence of people in a better position to know the true identity of the people involved in the takeover of Bratunac, so the Prosecution would submit that it is not necessary under 92 bis for this witness to be called for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the -- the Glogova incident, the massacre, as it's said?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A large number of people. But we have had witnesses about -- we've had this witness who gave evidence about the execution on the river bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That was 1701. And again, he testified about seeing men in JNA uniforms. The accused challenged that. It is unlikely that this particular witness can advance that point any further. And as I've said, the Prosecution plans to call at least one witness who will be able to -- will be available for both examination-in-chief and cross-examination on this issue and is in a better position to know who was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I think that leaves 1502, and you concede again cross-examination there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Kay, in those circumstances, is there anything you want to -- to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The amici have put in a detailed filing of the arguments upon the matter. Obviously the Prosecution have had time to reflect on their initial motion and submission and have conceded the cross-examination issue on a major part of those witnesses. Those that they don't concede cross-examination upon, there's nothing further for me to add because the material is already within that filing. And as I have identified in our reply, those witnesses were cumulative of other evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, do you want to say anything about these particular witnesses? Any argument you want to address on that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing specific, except that in their case too we are confronted with the same problem and that is limiting the possibility of establishing the truth and of cross-examining the witnesses, shortening the time with 92 bis witnesses, protected witnesses, and a series of other points that I have already raised which apply to this group of witnesses as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider the matter. We'll give our ruling on Tuesday, when we next sit. Yes. Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the first witness being brought in this morning is Mr. Emil Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, would you take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Emil Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And Mr. Cakalic, did you previously testify here at the Tribunal in the case of Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to offer the transcript of the witness's testimony from that trial into evidence under Rule 92 bis (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got here what seems to be a bundle of his papers or a bundle of exhibits; is that right? Are you asking to have anything more than the transcript admitted at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're asking for also the exhibits found at tab 2, which were Exhibits 51, 52, and 53, tendered during his testimony. I will not be asking him any questions about those this morning, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will give it a single exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 504.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, I'm going to summarise now the testimony that you gave on that previous occasion. I'll interrupt that summary on a few occasions to ask you some questions about areas that weren't covered in your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: The witness is a Croatian man who was 57 years old at the time of the events in question. During the battle for Vukovar, his job was to ensure good quality drinking water for the population and army and hygienically correct food for the Croatian army and police. On the 17th of November, 1991, the witness learned that units of the Yugoslav army and paramilitary units had boarded inhabitants from the street in which he lived in personnel carriers and taken them away. The witness and his wife decided to abandon their home and go to the Vukovar hospital. On 20 November 1991, at about 7.30 or 8.00 in the morning, all employees of the hospital were called to a meeting. All others who were not employed in the hospital were asked to leave through emergency ward doors. There were about 250 people gathered there. There were two soldiers there, including one named Pero, that the witness later saw when he was being taken from Vukovar to Sremska Mitrovica. This soldier, Pero, was cursing them and said that he would kill all of them if there were not prisoners in Croatian hands who were members of his army. There were five busses outside the hospital. After being searched and having anything dangerous taken away, JNA soldiers ordered them to get on the busses. They drove to the military barracks in Vukovar. There soldiers and people identified by the witness as Chetniks mistreated them psychologically, saying things like, "I'm going to slaughter you," or, "I'm going to cut your throat." The busses stayed at the barracks until approximately 2.00 in the afternoon. From there they went to Ovcara. They were met at Ovcara by a captain of the Yugoslav army. After the captain took personal possessions from them, including the witness's eyeglasses, which were smashed, everyone on the busses had to pass between two rows of these Chetniks, who beat everyone, including Dr. Bosanac's father-in-law, who was over 70 at the time. Inside the hangar, the beatings intensified. The witness himself was beaten with a wooden crutch, causing serious injury to his vertebrae. The witness saw two men beaten so badly in the hangar that they were killed. Inside the hangar, a man appeared, strong, big, with a large cap and a big cockade on it. He was with a major who was being called Major Milan Lukic. The major wanted to use an electric baton on the prisoners, but the other man warned him not to do that because there were too many witnesses. After Ovcara, the witness saw this same major in Negoslavci, when this major was escorting the witness's convoy from Vukovar to Sremska Mitrovica. After some time, a man dressed in a JNA uniform called the witness outside of the hangar. There were seven people gathered there. The beatings continued inside the hangar, but outside the witness saw the soldiers who had escorted them in the busses looking for money. After some time, the witness was called back into the hangar where a colonel and two lieutenant colonels took down his particulars. He was then put into a kombi van and driven away. From Ovcara, the witness was taken to the Velepromet in Vukovar. There was no room there, so they were transferred to a privately owned tailoring company called Modateks. Several of the people he was being held with were beaten, and one sergeant major threatened to have a man named Topola burn out the eyes of one of the prisoners with a cigarette butt. I'd like to jump to paragraph 13 of the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, the people who were beating the prisoners at Modateks, could you tell, based on the uniforms they were wearing, whether these were JNA soldiers, or were they something else?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They were JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And this person that was referred to, Topola, who they threatened to use to burn out the eyes of the prisoners with a cigarette butt, did you see Topola at Ovcara before you arrived at the Modateks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Returning to the summary, Your Honour, paragraph 8. The witness remained at Modateks until the 21st, when he was taken back on foot to the Velepromet warehouse. At the Velepromet, everything the witness had was taken away from him. He was taken into a room called the room of death. During that night, several people were taken away from this room and never returned. Your Honour, moving to paragraph 14 of the proofing summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell the Court how many people were taken out of the room of death, beaten, and never heard from again?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Six people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And, sir, were you able to actually hear the beatings that took place and the conversations that took place outside of this room? And if so, could you tell the Court what you heard.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: When they took out a graduate agricultural engineer, the director of the Vukovar slaughterhouse, he was called out and he was taken outside. This room, this room of death, had a window with bars, or rather, just bars without glass so that we could hear what was being said. They interrogated him where the meat was, where the wheat was, and then a blow could be heard, probably on his head, and then everything stopped. He was exhumed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, sir, about one prisoner who was brought back into the room of death, after being questioned, with cigarette burns on his body. Could you tell the Court about that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Wilhelm Karlovic is his name. He's now still in the Croatian army. He has the rank of major. He was taken out twice and brought back. On his body, they would extinguish their cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Could you -- when he came back into the room, could you see the marks on his body where the cigarettes were extinguished?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only on a part of his body, because he was wearing clothes. He was stripped and they made these cigarette burns all over his body, but then he put on his clothes, so we only saw them on his arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Were there JNA soldiers present at this room of death? And if so, approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were three of them that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: In addition to the JNA soldiers, were there any of these people that you've referred to as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There are some people from Vukovar that I knew, that I had collaborated with. For instance, Zarko Leskovac, who had hand grenades on his chest and automatic rifle. He was always tipsy. He would demand that the door be opened of the room of death. He would leave, and then after that certain people would be called out, some of whom never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: You said that he would call to have the door opened to the room of death. Who was it that could actually open that room? Who had the key to that room?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: One of those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: When you say "soldiers," are you referring to JNA soldiers or someone else?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The soldiers of the JNA, yes. That's how they introduced themselves. That is what they said they were, special policemen in the Yugoslav army, military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And this Topola that you said was at Ovcara, did you also see him at the Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I did. First of all, I saw him at Ovcara and later on at the Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honours, returning to the proofing summary, paragraph 10. During the night, a captain of the counterintelligence service came and took the witness and others to the JNA barracks because he said that if he didn't do this, the Chetniks would kill them all. As it came closer to morning, military policemen arrived and they began to beat individuals there. One man had his hands tied and was made to swallow two or three bullets. Question from paragraph 15 of the summary:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court who it was that was beating the prisoners at the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The Muslims had declared themselves as being Muslims, and the soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army. So they were military policemen too of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Turning to paragraph 11 of the proofing summary. As morning dawned, a soldier arrived and introduced himself as Captain Vojin Mesic, a Serb from Negoslavci. After dividing the Serbs from the Croats, this captain turned to the Croats and said, "Listen, we are going to kill all of you. We are going to burn you and throw your ashes into the Danube to destroy your Croat seed." The witness and the others were put on a bus and shipped to Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia, stopping in Negoslavci along the way. And a question from paragraph 16 about this stop in Negoslavci: Sir, this JNA major that you saw at Ovcara, the one who threatened to use an electric baton and was called by the name of Milan Lukic, did you see this major again at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him in Negoslavci; however, they didn't call him Lukic; they called him Ivanovic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, would you clarify one thing before we go any further. The reference to the Muslims who were doing the beating at the JNA barracks. It may be clear to some, but it's not clear what that is a reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, at the JNA barracks, you referred to Muslims who did some of the beatings at the JNA barracks. Could you tell us what military organisation, if any, these Muslims were affiliated with and how it is that you concluded that they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were both Muslims and Serbs, but these said for themselves that they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Who were they? What were they doing in the barracks? Could you just explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were stationed there, and they were military policemen of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Returning for a moment to Negoslavci, when you saw this major. Did you overhear what his job was in the JNA and why he was at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There was a whole convoy, in fact, and they were driving. There were tanks in front, where there were some doctors in the tanks. And he was escorting, one of the escorts of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Returning to the proofing summary, paragraph 12. Upon the witness's arrival at Sremska Mitrovica, he was interrogated by Boro Savic and Goran Hadzic, and while in Sremska Mitrovica the witness was beaten severely and suffered serious injuries. That is the end of the summary, Your Honour. I have just a few additional questions about Sremska Mitrovica covered in paragraphs 17, 18, and 19 of the proofing summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, upon your arrival at Sremska Mitrovica, did you have to pass through a double row of military police officers similar to the cordon that you had to go through at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- we had to run the gauntlet and there were a lot of them. There are three steps up and three steps down through a metal door that you have to go through, and they were lined up, the blue policemen, with their batons and clubs. And they were standing about 3 to 4 metres apart, and everybody beat us any way they could until we arrived in the playground, where they lined us up and asked us what our names were, what we did, and anything we did, they said we'd been doing the wrong things, "You were a baker, you baked bread. You were a cobbler, you repaired shoes." And we were beaten up very badly there. There was a Muslim there who was doing the beating along with a Serb, and I heard him say, "Yes, I'm a Muslim, but I'm a member of the Yugoslav People's Army." And the other one said, "I'm a Serb." And there were 37 of us, I think, there and there were about 50 of the policemen there, maybe more, I couldn't count them all. But they all beat us after these two. And we had to lie down on the ground, and they beat us one by one. It was absolutely unbelievable. People fell down, they couldn't get up afterwards. When they did manage to get up, they would fall to the ground again. It was absolutely terrible. Many of them lay there unconscious. I, too, was badly beaten. They especially liked to beat us on the head and neck, where it's most sensitive, because you have your central nervous system going down your backbone and spine, so they had probably received instructions that that's where they were to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. beat us, and they did it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And during these beatings, did you see a prisoner beaten to death?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That was a little later on. The beating went on two more times, and then towards night they wanted to take us into the rooms, 10 by 10, approximately. Suddenly there was some confusion, and I saw them kill Niko Soljic. Some 15 to 20 minutes later, they brought in a coffin, put him inside the coffin, and drove him away, killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Sir, approximately how many times were you personally beaten at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I counted up to 20 times and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And you referred to being questioned at one point by Boro Savic and Goran Hadzic. At the time that you were being questioned by them, did you recognise another man from Vukovar standing there carrying a baseball bat? And if so, who was that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was a judge in the Vukovar court, and his name was Branko Kovacevic. He stood guard by the door for Goran Hadzic and Boro Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, who it was that ran this prison at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Most probably it was a colonel, but anyway, it was the Yugoslav People's Army that had control of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And did local non-JNA paramilitaries ever come into this prison? And if so, when would they come in, in general?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was the Vukovar men who would usually turn up, usually on a Saturday and Sunday, when the army wasn't there. And then they would call people out and take them off, individuals from the camp. They would take them into rooms, put socks on their heads so that people couldn't recognise them, and then proceeded to beat those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. That's all the questions that I have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cakalic, did you or were you in any way involved in the Croatian National Guards corps in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was a sanitary inspector in Vukovar, and I saw that there were problems with water supplies and food supplies, and I volunteered and went to the defence office on the 15th of June. I reported there and said that as a professional I'd be happy to do that job for the Croatian army, for the police, and for all the citizens of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say you never had any -- actually, you were involved in the ZNG but you had no post or position within the organisation, did you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. As you controlled the food, among other things, you did food inspection - and I can see from the statement that you gave to the representative of the MUP of Croatia in May 1992 that you inspected the food in Dunav and the Gradiska Kafana and some other facilities.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and others too. I don't know whether you know the Grand building in Vukovar. It's the workers centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you conducted the food inspection.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, except in Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Except in Borovo Naselje. Right. Now, how many meals did you have to inspect per day?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I had a system. I devised a system by which all the employees working there - there were Croatian ladies and Serbian ladies and Muslim ladies - and I required that they disinfect all the cutlery and glasses and cups and the dishes in which food was transported to the battlefield. And each of them had to eat that food before they sent it on to the soldiers, and they did eat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So as you sent food to the battlefield, how many people were these meals prepared for?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, transport was something else. Other people dealt with that. This was just the preparation, the cooking of food, whereas the transport was conducted in special vehicles by other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So if you controlled all this and inspected it all, you can't actually tell us of the quantity of food and for how many people the food was being cooked for.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I understand it, before the war, before the conflict broke out, you also worked in the municipality of Vukovar as head of the sanitary inspection team.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I wasn't the chief, the boss; I was a sanitary inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. That means you were an employee of the Vukovar municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when in July 1991 there was a decree disbanding the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar, which had been regularly elected at the free elections which were held, when the others were there, and that the then-president was suspended? His name was Slavko Dokmanovic, wasn't it, and he was the mayor or president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He continued to work, and I cooperated with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And as a commissioner of the Croatian government, it was Marin Vidic, Bili, who was appointed.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he took over the role of president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was a representative of the government of the Republic of Croatia for the municipality of Vukovar. That's what his post was called, his position. But I can tell you that after the situation in Borovo Selo, when those 13 policemen were killed over there, representatives of the International Red Cross arrived, and I think it was Dr. Nicholson, along with the president of the Yugoslav Red Cross and the president of the Croatian Red Cross, and I think we went to Borovo because that representative of the International Red Cross wanted to see what the situation was like for himself and what had happened there. And we were driven there in armoured cars. But after some time had gone by, a former policemen turned up. I knew him well, I was on good terms, and he said, "Emil, get away from here as quick as you can. Leave here, leave this place."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the point of that, of what you're saying? There were civilians over there.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were Chetniks and there were also several members, as far as I was able to see, about ten of them in fact, with some strange caps on their heads, and they were about 50 to 60 metres away from us and they would run across from one side of the road to the other, probably to instil fear in us, so that we thought there were more of them than there actually were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many do you mean strange caps?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, Chetnik caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they weren't members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Markovic was there at a rally, the president of Yugoslavia, I mean, and he attended a rally where there were members of the Yugoslav People's Army before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Ante Markovic? Is that who you mean? And he was the Prime Minister of the federal government, as you know, and as you know he was a Croat himself.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the Prime Minister of the federal government comes to any place, you would have the citizens rally.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that it was always like that. I myself didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could have gone if you wanted to.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: But luckily, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Not to dwell on that for too long. Tell me, please: As you were an employee of the municipality yourself, I'm sure you know that Marin Vidic, Bili -- you knew him personally, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we collaborated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then you knew him personally and cooperated. I'm sure you will know, then, that in the second half of May already in 1990 in the area of Lovas.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That's his native village

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, his native village. Anyway, he formed a military organisation within the HDZ party and divided it up into the technical service, at whose head we had Ivo Madzarevic, and the military service --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if the witness knows anything about any of this. Mr. Cakalic, do you know anything about any of this that's being alleged by the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm hearing this for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never heard of that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No point going into detail about that. He doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I expected you to interrupt me, although the witness said that he knew him well, Marin Vidic and cooperated with him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then there was no need to ask the question if you were expecting interruption. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you've been misled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm going to ask the witness something now. Vukovar isn't a large town, you know, and I'm going to ask him whether he knew Marin Vidic. And as you can see, he knows where he was born, and it was the village of Lovas, and he knew about Lovas in 1990. And I have here a court document from the military court in Belgrade and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This has nothing to do -- Do you know anything about the military court in Belgrade, Mr. Cakalic? Of course he doesn't. It's nothing to do with the witness. Now, if you want to get some evidence in about Mr. Vidic, Bili, then you can try later, but there's no point abusing the process by putting something to a witness which he knows nothing about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I really believe that the witness doesn't know anything about the military court in Belgrade. And indeed I'm not asking him about the military court in Belgrade. I'm asking him about something that has to do with a document of the military court in Belgrade and I'm asking him whether he knows about the events referred to there. And I imagine I should not be forbidden to ask him questions about what he himself had said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can put the matter, put it shortly, and we'll see if the witness knows anything about it, what the allegation is. You can certainly put that from the document you have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Ivo Madzarevic and did you know him?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Markica Gracanac?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Franjo Mujic, at least, who was in charge of this medical service? Because you are from that line of work.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: In Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Franjo Mujic, Branko Krizmanic, do you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: None of them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, not by their name or surnames. Perhaps I know them by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the organisation of this armed formation within the HDZ as far back as 1990 in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I first heard of it from you just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything about the collection of money to buy weapons then, that is to say, as far back as 1990?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Everybody bought weapons for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, nothing was collected. Everybody bought their own weapons?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Everybody bought their own weapons. Who wanted to buy a rifle, brought his own rifle. You know that the entire civilian defence had been disarmed and the Secretariat of National Defence, with all their weapons, all of that was disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the price of an automatic rifle at that time? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, at first it cost about 2.000 Deutschmark, afterwards 1.000 Deutschmark, and then 500 Deutschmark, and afterwards you could get them for free.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume hat you did not buy a rifle.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was not your activity?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those people who were buying rifles, who were they buying them from?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: From smugglers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was involved in the organisation of this armed smuggling; a person you know from the territory of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember -- I mean, I assume that you know Tomislav Mercep.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I do him know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was Secretary for National Defence in the municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was appointed precisely by Marin Vidic, Bili, when he took over as representative of the Croatian government in Vukovar. He was the one who appointed him chief of National Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Vidic appointed him, but he was head of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I hear that Vidic appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was involved in the formation of precisely those military units, those military units that were within the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: As for that question, I could not answer it, because it wasn't formation within the HDZ. It was within the defence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you know Josip Gazo?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did he do?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was -- when I came from camp, I found him in Zagreb. And he was chief of police when I was in Zagreb then, after being in camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember within that organisation, that is to say, Marin Vidic, Tomislav Mercep, this chief of police you mentioned just now, and so on and so forth, do you remember what happened in terms of the activities that directly threatened the safety of persons and property?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: This chief of police was not in Vukovar. He was chief of police when the entire government was moved to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To Zagreb, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Mercep's activities? This had to do with the fact that many Serbs went missing or were killed in Vukovar before these operations.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear that Serbs were killed in Vukovar. This is the first time I ever hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is a court document, can I have it exhibited? Because obviously the witness recognises some of the persons mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's nothing to do with the witness, absolutely nothing to do with him at all. The fact that he's heard of somebody mentioned in a document is not a ground for exhibiting it. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, what is going on here has nothing to do with me either, but here I am, and I'm carrying out these activities that really have nothing to do with me whatsoever. But if you believe that this has nothing to do with the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just get on with it. If you have any questions for the witness, or we'll let him go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at least the following: That on the 3rd of September, 1991 a decision was reached precisely in the municipality of Vukovar and precisely by Mercep and precisely by Vidic ordering the directors of Electroslavonija, the water supply company, and the PTT to cut off electricity, water, and telephone from the military barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me the date, please? I haven't remembered --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mercep was no longer in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about these people who headed the service, the people he appointed. Rimac Vlado headed the technical service and Gazo Josip headed the military service. Stipan Radas. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Obviously you got something confused there, sir. After the month of September -- rather, after the month of August, Mercep was not in Vukovar any more at all. He was transferred to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To Zagreb, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Dedakovic, Mile Dedakovic, Colonel Dedakovic took over the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the people he appointed. Do you know Vlado Rimac, Gazo Josip, and Stipan Radas?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I know Gazo Josip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this decision was reached on the 3rd of September? I'm talking about these people here appointed. And Mercep was with John Tuzaga [phoen] precisely at the request of Marin Vidic because he had committed crimes there.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, that's not the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the letter that Marin Vidic wrote to Tudjman about this?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't have that letter. But I'll tell you one thing: Mercep was not a military man. He was not an expert in these matters. He was an engineer. It was Dedakovic who was a military man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I'm asking you whether you know about this decision of the 3rd of September -- or rather, this order that was issued to the director of Electroslavonija, that is the power supply company in Vukovar, is that right, and the water supply company, and the PTT to have electricity, water, and telephone lines cut off from the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: When the entire population had their electricity, power, et cetera cut off, that is when this happened to the military barracks too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which date was this?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. I think it was sometime in the second half of September, something like that, around the second half of the month of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that precisely then this Mile Dedakovic, Jastreb, with the so-called active service of the ZNG surrounded the Vukovar military barracks and started the blockade of the barracks and started opening fire at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The barracks was being surrendered. I don't know whether you know about that. They had a white flag put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened before this white flag was put up?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was no blockade, no gunfire, no shooting, nothing?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was agreed upon that no problems should be made, otherwise this barracks should not be surrendered. And these barracks could have fallen very easily, however, obviously orders had come from someone in Belgrade that the barracks should not be surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the barracks was supposed to be surrendered and then --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Like all others in Croatia. Like all others in Croatia that were being surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then orders came from someone in Belgrade that they should not be surrendered, and then --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, from Belgrade or from Negoslavci, I don't know about that, but obviously somebody sent an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Cakalic. Let's just clarify this matter: You claim that there was no blockade, no shooting at the barracks, that a white flag was put up and that the barracks was supposed to be surrendered and that the fighting started later.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was not present there, so I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about the order? Because it was issued to all office-holders in Vukovar, and you were sanitary inspector there. And this was done as far back as the 8th of September, 1991, that is to say, being on the ready, taking measures for readiness at the first degree, second degree, third level, rather, of the readiness. The third level of readiness restricts the movement of citizens in terms of time, and certain units are activated and so on and so forth. Were you made aware of this order? There is a series of persons here who signed their names stating that they were familiarised with the order. This probably doesn't include your signature, but maybe you could recognise some of the other people. This is an order issued by Marin Vidic, Bili. This is the original language and could you just take a look at this and see whether you know any of the signators of this document.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll take a look. As for these signatures, I could not decipher them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just have a look at the document. Mr. Cakalic, do you recognise the document itself? Do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a logical document. A certain government authority drafted this and warned all citizens of Vukovar that their movement is being restricted because Vukovar was being shelled and bombed all the time, and it was logical. All people were made aware of this. It's not only Croats; it's the entire population of Vukovar that was made aware of this. I don't know whether you know that Vukovar had 25 different ethnic groups amongst its population and town. Most of them were Croats, then Serbs, then all the rest. This is quite logical. Immediate preparations should be carried out in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand all of this. Just look at the date, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was Vukovar bombed?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date when it was bombed, but I was in town. I went to inspect food at the workers centre and at the hotel, and that's when aircraft were flying and gunning the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Gunning what?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Gunning down the citizens of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Aircraft were flying and shooting at the 27 different ethnic groups of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me or you don't want to understand me. The airplanes of your state that often came to Vukovar during the day and during the night shot at the population. Did you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. But when was this, sir? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date. From the month of September onwards, that happened every day. As a matter of fact, they even threw poison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Cakalic. But at that time, it was my state and your state too. It wasn't only mine.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The referendum had already taken place, and it was your state, and I don't know who would attack his own state, and you were attacking it then, and I don't know who would attack his own state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you see the aircraft shooting people, Mr. Cakalic, yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was repeated almost every day, until the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You cannot say when this happened.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say it started around the month of September. I cannot tell you exactly. It's not that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I really cannot give you the exact date. Far be it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that as early as February 1991, that is to say, half a year or perhaps more than half a year before there was any kind of unrest or any kind of conflicts in Vukovar, at a meeting of the HDZ in Cerpinska Cest [phoen] and Borovo Naselje a decision was passed to ethnically cleanse Serbs in the territory of the municipality of Vukovar? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. I did not belong to that political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mercep -- is Mercep from Bogdanovci?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I think he lived in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he did have a house in Bogdanovci?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, he and his brothers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about the meeting held in that house in Bogdanovci? At that time, Vladimir Seks was there, Ivan Vekic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, this is a waste of time, a total waste of time. You have now spent at least, if not over, half your time without asking this witness a single question about his evidence. He has narrated serious matters which happened to him and not a word of it have you challenged. If you're challenging it, you should do so now instead of dealing with matters which are totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll hurry up, and I understand that you find all of this irrelevant, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In particular with this witness who knows nothing about it but who's come here to give serious evidence which you're refusing to cross-examine for some reason.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not refusing to cross-examine him at all, Mr. May. I'm not refusing to cross-examine him about his evidence but first I'm putting questions to him that have to do with the situation in Vukovar the time that his statement refers to, and these are circumstances under which all of this happened, and I believe all of this is relevant, as opposed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the name of Cibaric Nikola, nicknamed Sipka [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Sipos Zoran?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Not Sipos, but Cibaric I knew, and I still know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the war operations that there was a shelter at the Borovo factory and it was called Novo Bucara [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. Commerc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was a shelter in the Borovo factory by that name?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, that this Cibaric Nikola from this shelter and this other man who you don't know, that they took Serbs out of this shelter, liquidated them, shot them dead?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have a minute -- a document here, minutes of the information received, and it refers to Novo Bucara?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He knows nothing about this, so move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that cannot be tendered either. Very well, Mr. May, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about specifically on the 14th in 1991 people were taken out of this shelter and executed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you continue with these questions, the cross-examination will be brought to an end. You've been told that he knows nothing about it. It's irrelevant to him, irrelevant to us now. Now, move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were a sanitary inspector, are you aware of Marin Vidic's decision from September 1991 that the bodies of JNA soldiers should not be buried in Vukovar but that they should be burned?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I'm not even aware of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Cakalic, you and your wife arrived at the Vukovar hospital on the 17th of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At 2300 hours?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 2, you say that most Croats from your building went to the hospital and that all the Serbs and one Ukrainian remained in their apartments; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they were with us all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you yourself say, Vukovar was endangered by shelling; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Shells don't choose whether they will hit a Serb, a Ukrainian, or a Croat, I assume.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a Serb to kill me -- he was assigned the task of killing me, and he was killed by his own shell. He didn't know this could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just saying that you were threatened by shells used to bomb Vukovar, and the Croats went to seek shelter in the hospitals, whereas those same shells did not endanger the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That day there was very little shooting, and when my wife and I -- I don't know whether you're familiar with Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, or maybe fortunately, I was never there.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We were walking and they were shooting, sir, shooting. You understand? I was driving a wounded man the day before to the hospital. He had been wounded. And on my way back, they started shooting at me. I switched off the lights and moved to the side, and there were bullets whizzing by. You have no idea how it was. And this was coming from the right bank of the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But let us cover these questions quickly, because my time is limited. Do you have any explanation for the fact that the Serbs did not seek shelter in the hospital? Was the hospital accessible only to Croats as shelter or to everyone?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. They were safe. They had been informed what would happen and how it would happen. And let me tell you that when we were taken to Ovcara they didn't even check the identity of people and they even killed some Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll come to that in a moment. Just tell me, please: You are not linking this failure of the Serbs being admitted to the hospital with a position of the director of the hospital, Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, that has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, page 4, you say that in the hospital you saw Marin Vidic, the government representative for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I was close by when Major Sljivancanin arrested him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, when did a JNA officer enter the hospital for the first time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Then, when Marin was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim it was Major Sljivancanin, and he was accompanied by a warrant officer whose name was Bogdan Kuzmic.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he a reservist, a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He used to be the porter at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste time. I assume you know that a lieutenant in the JNA has to be a graduate of the military academy. So he couldn't have been a porter at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: But you interrupted me. I was just going to say that. He was the porter at the hospital, the receptionist. He was escorting Major Sljivancanin when Vukovar was surrendered, when Vidic was arrested. I heard later on that he was taken to Belgrade for additional training to the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's something else. If he wanted to become an active officer later on. But in those days, he was a member of the TO of Vukovar, and he was Major Sljivancanin's guide because he used to work as a receptionist in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Sir, no. He was wearing the uniform of the JNA with the ranks that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the Territorial Defence wore the same, or maybe you don't know that. On page 5 of your statement, you say that it became immediately clear to you that Sljivancanin was in charge of the operation.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you were in charge of it; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what kind of operation was Sljivancanin carrying out?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The arrest of Marin Vidic at 00 hours on the 19th. And then I saw him again on the 19th around 7.00, 7.30 maybe, or 7.00 roughly, him and Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that his behaviour was correct and that he didn't resort to any kind of violence?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was correct. What I was able to see when he arrested Vidic and when he took him away from the hospital, yes. I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Vidic was later taken to the investigating court?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we met again in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see any other JNA members on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I said that I saw Captain --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, this receptionist.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, no, Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And is it true that Dr. Ivankovac and Dr. Matos on the 20th of November informed you that all persons without official IDs have to leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vesna Bosanac and some others informed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that they would be transferred in a convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They didn't tell us where we would be transferred. However, I know where I was transferred, and you do too probably, and many others. My wife was also taken to Sremska Mitrovica and then returned to Croatia later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you know who Dr. Vladimir Emedi is? Is he a doctor at the Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, an orthopaedic surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please: In view of the fact that before the 17th of November, 1991, as you yourself say, you did go to the hospital, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see in it armed members of the ZNG, and how many of them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No one. I didn't see anyone armed in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this doctor that you say you knew, Vladimir Emedi --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I still know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Said in his statement that Dr. Vesna Bosanac was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can put some fact which this witness might know about, but he doesn't know about the statement of some other witness that you may have had or some statement that you've got. What is -- what is the allegation that you want to put? We'll see if this witness can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of the National Guards Corps, with the permission of the director of the hospital, Vesna Bosanac, were staying at the hospital, climbed to the roof of the hospital, from which they opened fire on JNA positions, on aircraft of the JNA, et cetera? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: And what were those aircraft doing in Vukovar? Shelling the hospital? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, if you could just concentrate on the question. When are you saying this happened, Mr. Milosevic? When is it that you say the ZNG were firing from the roof of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout that period, up until the fall of Vukovar -- after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, did you see anything like that yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it was impossible to climb to the roof of the hospital, because the hospital had already received a couple of shells. A 250-kilogramme bomb had fallen through the second, first floor and the ground floor and fell between the legs of a wounded man, and it didn't go off. Who would have dared to climb onto the roof of the hospital in those days? That is unbelievable. I hear that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hear what you are saying for the first time too, but I have information that from the roof of the hospital fire was opened on planes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He's denied it. He has denied it, so let's not waste further time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming you didn't see any members of the ZNG within the hospital.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: You asked me on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't climb to the roof.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: You're asking me whether I saw them on the roof, whether they were members of the ZNG firing at Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see them in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was in the hospital for only three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, not a single one. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you recognise a certain number who had put on hospital uniforms that did not belong to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise them. Do you know how I recognised them? In the busses. They were wearing white coats and they were all killed straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those who were wearing white coats and who were not hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After you left the hospital and went into the yard, you say you noticed two soldiers, one whose name was Pero from Bosnia and another one who was a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know them from before?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. I saw them for the first time on that occasion. But they were polite young men who cursed us from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you didn't know them from before, how did you know who was who, who's a Serb, who's a Muslim, and so on? They were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: This Pero escorted us in the convoy from Vukovar to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in the bus you said that next to you was Tomislav Pap; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sitting next to you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the person who, following Vidic's instructions, was burning the bodies of killed JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Sir, I never heard of the burning of corpses in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. If you don't know about it, we'll move on. On page 7, you say that you were taken from the hospital to the barracks compound, where, as you say - and you mentioned that again a moment ago - you were insulted, threatened --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Not just me; everyone was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said by some Chetniks of Montenegrin ethnicity; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know what ethnicity they were. They wore those little red caps with fringes. Where are they from? Are they from Bosnia? Are they from Montenegro? Are they from Serbia? Are they from Croatia? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those red caps with fringes are not worn in Serbia but in some parts of Croatia they are.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they're the caps worn in Lika, but that's something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the Montenegrin one doesn't have these fringes. And is it true that you recognised some other people in the barracks, some local Serbs from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you had known them before the war too.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And from there you were transferred to Ovcara; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I won't ask you anything about the glasses. You mentioned a captain -- so as not to waste time on that. In 1993, you gave a statement to -- I think it was a lady, Kim Carter, something like that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. She's a colonel of the Canadian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: And she is a member of the Council of the International Court, I think she was. And also present was a gentleman, the pathologist who discovered Ovcara. I can't remember his surname now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Let's not waste time. This is quite a lengthy statement and --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: His name was Snow Clyde, I just remembered, the pathologist's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this captain on page 38 who was trying on glasses, et cetera, and you say he was a captain by rank. And then you say, "Probably a reservist."

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I didn't know whether he was active duty or a reservist. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading out what you said. I'm not suggesting that he was a reservist, I'm just reading what you said. You said, "Probably a reservist, and I saw that he couldn't button up his uniform."

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Because it didn't fit him. It didn't fit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, it didn't fit him. As opposed to other officers.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in some other assertions here you say that those men were dirty, disorderly, et cetera. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. We, too, were rather dirty and messy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, is it clear from that that these were people who were not members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Sir, they were wearing JNA uniforms. Whether they belonged or not, I don't know. I don't know whether you know whether they belonged or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I certainly don't know, but I assume, on the basis of the information I have, there were no JNA members at all at Ovcara, because it was -- these were local -- of course uniformed but local members of the armed forces, and that is why I'm asking you, because that's what I'm trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There were three officers - one colonel and two lieutenant colonels - in Ovcara, and they were in charge of the whole parade that was happening over there, and another 12, up to 15 men came with baseball bats in a separate vehicle. And when they entered Ovcara, the gates closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you're saying that the commander in the hospital was Major Sljivancanin, and here you're mentioning one colonel and two lieutenant colonels. Please separate the hospital from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do not interrupt the witness. Can you -- just a moment. Yes, go on, Mr. Cakalic. Let him finish. Just one at a time. Do you know -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask for pauses, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sljivancanin was in the hospital, and Sljivancanin appeared in the Vukovar barracks when they took us there from the hospital. And when we reached Ovcara, two lieutenant colonels and a colonel appeared, who came from somewhere. They appeared there after Dokmanovic had left from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to you for this. So we've established that Sljivancanin arrested Vidic, and he was anyway a security officer. He behaved correctly. And he took Vidic away. Vidic was later in prison and later -- it doesn't matter, for your evidence. So you didn't see Sljivancanin in Ovcara at all.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: In Ovcara, no, but in the barracks, yes. He came to see us in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A major in the barracks, it was only logical for him to be there. Now you are saying two colonels and one lieutenant colonel. Do you have any idea as to how they could have been active JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have an idea. Did you see the magazine Nasa Armija from the end of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was on the front page of that magazine? Mile -- what's his name, Mrksic. He liberated Vukovar. And I identified him when I received that magazine in Mitrovica. They gave us that magazine to read, and I compared him with the colonel who came to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And just -- let's clarify that. And it's in fact, time for the adjournment. You say you identified him. You identified him as the colonel, is that right, at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.
