utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes. Mr. Cakalic, don't speak to anybody about your -- to anybody about your evidence until it's over. And would you be back in 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much more time do I have, Mr. May? [In English] How much time? [Interpretation] I was asking you how much more time will you give me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, 12 minutes isn't enough. Twelve minutes isn't enough for this witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A quarter of an hour and then we'll consider the position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, but I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, I would like us to establish the truth of actually what happened there, so could you give me precise answers to the questions I'm asking you. You said that you recognised Colonel Mrksic. Did you recognise him on the basis of the photograph you later saw on that cover page of the magazine and you described him on the basis of the photograph or on the basis of what you saw over there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: When he entered Ovcara, the hangar of Ovcara, then a man came up, a soldier, and he said to the Chetniks there, Kuzmic and the others, said, "Colonel Mrksic is coming." There were two lieutenant colonels and one colonel so it was logical that Mrksic was the colonel. That's right, isn't it? And when I was in Sremska Mitrovica in the camp there, we got the magazines Nasa Armija and Front, two magazines to read. And when I got this Nasa Armija, "Our Army" magazine, on the cover was this man whom I recognised as being Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he have a whistle?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I was outside the hangar, and somebody had a whistle and gave the order for when they were supposed to start beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One witness, he was a protected witness so I can't read his name out, he was 1171 - that was his code - he said that there was a colonel and he described him as being a fat man with a whistle. Colonel Mrksic is not a fat man.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who made that statement and testified. What I said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the colonel you saw, was he fat?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: There was a Chetnik who was fat. He was about 150 to 160 kilogrammes, and he owned the baton that the major held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you recognised some local Serbs who beat you, and among them Slavko Dokmanovic and a certain man called Milan Bulic, Dado Dukic, and Bogdan Kuzmic, as well as Stevan Miscevic.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that before the war in Vukovar they sold fish; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that man Miscevic, he's a fisherman, he sold his own fish. He caught the fish. He was a fisherman himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 9 you say you saw Kuzmic and Bulic beating a man called Samardzic, Damjan Samardzic at Ovcara, nicknamed Kemo?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: And they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that Kuzmic and Bulic were not members of the JNA, either of them? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, they were paramilitary units. They were in paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to establish. Right. Now, Mr. Cakalic, together with you in the bus, you mentioned a moment ago during the examination in chief Vilim Karlovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said in passing that he is a major in the Croatian army to this day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He's a major, a Bojnik, as they call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Bojnik, then, meaning major. Isn't it clear that thereby you are denying your assertion that in the hospital and with you there were no people who were members of the armed forces of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I didn't know he was in the army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't know he was in the army at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No. He was a patient in the hospital, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't suppose you're disputing the fact that he was in the army.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That's what I learnt later on, yes. I heard of that later..

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to establish, thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He's in the army today too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim at Ovcara a Serb member of the Territorial Defence by the name of Stevo Zoric, nicknamed Cevo, saved you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And throughout your statement you refer to Serbs in two ways; you either say "Chetniks" or you say "soldiers"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Do you call them anything else? Chetniks are one thing. They needn't only be Serbs. They can be Montenegrins too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Fine. But you, for instance, spoke about a certain major, and a moment ago when you spoke about that particular major you said that it was a major who had a large cockade, cap.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That's wrong. That's a mistake. No, that's not what I said. The major was given this electric baton from the Chetnik, the large one that I said weighed at least 130, 40 kilogrammes, 2 metres high. He had an enormous knife this big tucked into his belt, and that Chetnik said to that major, "Don't use it. There are a lot of witnesses, lots of eyewitnesses."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I thought I heard you say that the major with the large cockade was there.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood. The major is one man, the man with the cockade is another. They are two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We can check it out in the transcript, but we don't have time to do that now. You said that the major's name was Lukic and that later on he took the name of Ivanovic. So how do you explain this, him having two surnames?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Now, whether it was a pseudonym or not, I don't know. But the fact is that they called him -- one man came up and said, "Major Lukic is coming." Or rather, those three officers, the two lieutenant colonels and one colonel. "They're coming and let's go outside." That is what Lukic said. And when I heard him being called by his surname in Negoslavci, Major Ivanovic, I saw that it was one and the same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, either in the hospital or at Velepromet or at Ovcara did you see a single JNA soldier kill any of the detainees? I'm asking you whether you saw a single soldier, a single JNA soldier kill a single detainee.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that at Ovcara you noticed a young member of the Territorial Defence and you say that his name was Guja and the son of a Serb woman by the name of Mirjana Guga.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was the person who opened and closed the hangar and he was wearing the JNA uniform, not at Ovcara, not in the hangar itself, actually outside the hangar. He was in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In front of the hangar, right.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that he cursed your Ustasha grandmother and cursed his uncle who was a tradesman in Autobacka and said that he would kill him if the opportunity ever arose? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this young man, was his father a Croat?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And his surname was Molnar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, Molnar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the other surname was his mother's maiden name, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is what it says on -- in your statement. It says: "At the time, the military guard was held by Guja, and he swore at our Ustasha mother though he was a Croat himself, and he didn't like his uncle either." He said he'd kill him if the opportunity ever arose.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like to draw your attention, gentlemen, to how in this trial, in these proceedings, certain witnesses are being used who quite obviously have something to do with the crime and they are accusing innocent people, and those witnesses are being used as witnesses although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not the time for you to make submissions. Now, what is the question you want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in that same statement, on the page ending in number 86, when you described the people who beat the detainees in the hangar at Ovcara, that they used the term "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Chetniks of Vukovar, that was the expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these weren't members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That's right. This young man was outside the hangar. We've settled that one, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And is it true that you said that while you were at the Velepromet, in the room you were in, that a captain of the military police came into the room and told you to get ready to leave because the Chetniks could turn up at any moment ready to slaughter you all? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And I say the same thing here and now. "Do you want to tell me something else," he said. "Go on." He said, "Come on, people, I'll take you to the barracks because the Chetniks will come, they're all drunk and they'll kill you all." And he introduced himself as being Captain Kosa [phoen]. And I said, "Captain, do you give us your word that that's how it will be?" And he said yes. So we came to the yard and the busses, he couldn't switch the engines of the bus on and the Chetniks were coming in and he managed to switch the motor on and took us to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, I assume you differentiate between the representatives of the JNA and these people whom you say were drunk, and that there was the danger of them killing you there.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, I am deeply grateful to that captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you must pause. Pause for the interpreters, please, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you consider that had he handed you over, that you really would have been killed?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I do believe that I would have been killed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it quite clear that this representative of the JNA - it's not important what rank he had or anything else - for whom you say was a captain of the military police in fact saved your life?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was a KOS captain, counterintelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. A security captain. Well, it's the counterintelligence service, actually. That's the translation of KOS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: All right then. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you consider the captain saved your life?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he saved all our lives, all of us who survived that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, were you able to establish from that fact then that the JNA endeavoured to protect you under the circumstances and everything that was happening in Vukovar at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Not the JNA; it was that individual, sir, that particular KOS captain, who gave us his name and surname, which I'm afraid I haven't remembered. He was a little shorter than me. He was very proper and correct in his conduct and he said, "Come on, people. Get ready to leave. We've come to take you off in a bus and we'll take you all away from here." Whereas, the other members of JNA who were in the barracks behaved quite differently. First of all, they received us, gave us some water, something to eat, they took us in. And after that -- but I suppose you'll come to that. I don't want to jump the gun here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to you? Were you mistreated by the JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: In the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you said in the barracks there were members of some paramilitaries as well, paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't think you've understood me. I said I was taken prisoner in Vukovar hospital, taken to the barracks, from the barracks to Ovcara, from Ovcara to Velepromet, from Velepromet to Modateks, then back to Velepromet and from Velepromet with that captain, the KOS captain, taken back to the barracks. That was my route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And that captain saved you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did anything happen to any of you after that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It happened in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody killed in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Not in the barracks, no. But many guys were beaten, and a young boy of about 18 had to swallow bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But is it clear that the people whom you thought were coming to kill you were not members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The ones in the barracks were members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the ones who were in the barracks but the ones who were coming in to kill you and the ones that the captain of KOS saved you from.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He said that the Chetniks are coming. And when we got out of Velepromet to go into the busses, we heard their songs. You know the ones they sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But is it clear that the crime at Ovcara was not committed by members of the JNA? Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Oh, sir, I didn't watch them carry on killing. I just saw them kill Kemo and Damjan Samardzic in Ovcara itself. And we were driven off at around 7.00 from Ovcara to Velepromet, then Modateks, and then from Modateks back to Velepromet and then back to the barracks, as I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you've described that to us very well. So this officer of the JNA saved you. You and that group of men.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. And if you know him, say hello to him for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't know him personally. But he saved you from a band of men that could not have belonged to the JNA, a formation not belonging to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Those formations were members of the JNA, the ones that took us to the Velepromet were the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've stopped the -- I've stopped the microphone. You've now had rather more than the quarter of an hour we've promised. We've considered the situation in this case. We will give you another five minutes. We're not going to give you more because of the time that was spent and wasted earlier on on irrelevant cross-examination. You've got five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Cakalic. Now, can we clarify this: When you were taken over from Ovcara by the office of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Not from Ovcara, sir, from Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. From Velepromet, I mean. Then nobody after that was killed.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Right. Of the seven of us who were saved, that's who I'm talking about. The ones that stayed at Ovcara, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's another matter, yes. And there was no JNA formation there. I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a formation but there were those three officers, as I told you. That was at some other time, much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the JNA held the prison in Sremska Mitrovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The army?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you know that in Sremska Mitrovica there's a regular prison. Does that mean that part of the prison was handed over to these forces who brought in captives from Vukovar, detainees from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes, and from other places too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, did you have occasion to meet any representative of the authorities, except for the members of the army?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: The authorities, no. But journalists did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long were you in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: A little less than three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did they behave towards you in Sremska Mitrovica during those three months?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Differently at different times. For example, when we arrived in Sremska Mitrovica - and I've already said how we were beaten outside and then in the sports hall and then outside again --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned that. As far as I remember, you mentioned a paramilitary formation; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: You mean in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say paramilitary formation. Not at all. There were -- the highest rank I saw there was a colonel, and the lowest was a private -- a corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was his name, this --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I never learnt his name, and he didn't want to give us his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it was part of the prison used by the armed forces; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes. And before that, it was the condemned convicts who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did anything happen to anybody in Sremska Mitrovica? Was anybody killed?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Two or three minutes before midnight every night we would hear 10 to 15 shots fired. Every night. And the casualties in Sremska Mitrovica, when we were divided up into the rooms, I said Niko Soljic was killed. He was beaten to death, kicked to death in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who killed him?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, who could have been there in Sremska Mitrovica? Just the army, nobody else. No paramilitary units or anything of that kind could have been there, except on Saturdays and Sundays, the ones who came in from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you said that they would come from Vukovar when the army wasn't in the prison, when the soldiers weren't in the prison.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: It was like this: You couldn't leave a prison without the army; that is quite sure. But at that time, we didn't see a single officer or a single soldier in actual fact. They had withdrawn and gave a chance to these others to take it out on the people there. And if you ask me, it was the warden of the prison who was to blame, because they should have been governed by the international rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody is questioning that. But they were coming from Vukovar, and you say that Goran Hadzic was there - I made a note of that - Boro Savic, and Branko Kovacevic, a judge.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: But they didn't do the beating. They did the interrogation. I said they interviewed me, interrogated me, Goran Hadzic and Boro Savic, but that the guard in front of the door was Branko Kovacevic, a judge of the Vukovar court. So those two, the primitive people, he stood guard for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You even said that this judge had a baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Which judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this Branko Kovacevic. The judge that you say had a baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, he had a baton, a club, a white one, this big, a truncheon. Goran didn't beat me, neither did the other one. But when I was walking down the other corridor, that's when I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, it's not okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean it in that sense, all right? I meant it in the sense of your answer, of you having given me an answer. So these people who came from Vukovar to interrogate you, to question you, to talk to you, they did so to learn something, to get some information from you. Did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't beat me. I'm telling you this for the third time. Goran Hadzic or Boro Savic didn't beat me, nor did the judge beat me. When we were taken further away from them - and I think this was either in the basement or the ground floor - I was on the third floor, so between the ground floor, up the stairs to the third floor, that was when I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that Boro Savic or Goran Hadzic or this man Branko Kovacevic had anything to do with this mistreatment of you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what did they ask you? What kind of things did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: They asked me how many Serbs there were in the Croatian army, whether they had been mobilised. I said yes, they had been mobilised and I gave them the names and surnames of the people who had been mobilised. They were good soldiers, they asked me, were they? And I said, yes, they were good soldiers. One of them has an officer's pension today. He's retired with an officer's pension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic, your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many in all were there soldiers in Vukovar, of the Croatian ones, the Croatian National Guards Corps and all the rest of them? Because you told us how many Serbs there were in the army, I assume you know the Croats.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I know two of them, because they were from my own building. So I know these two particular ones. As to how -- what the total was, I really can't say. And I don't think it exists in the annals and records either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to ask the witness kindly to explain only a few things in relation to what happened in the hospital and around the hospital. That is why I would like to ask you, Your Honours, to look at tab 2, page 4, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the first thing I would like to ask you is the following: You were in the hospital on the 17th, 18th, and 19th, and on the 20th you left.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you again about all these things you already spoke of in relation to the appearance of Major Sljivancanin, but please look at page 4 of your statement, the one you gave to the investigators on the 18th of June, 1995. There is a sentence in that particular paragraph: "I personally did not see any other soldiers of the so-called JNA or Chetniks inside the hospital at that time." That's what you stated. Is that right? That during those three days you didn't?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't have been there because Vukovar had not fallen and the -- the hospital, rather, had not fallen. That's when they appeared, Sljivancanin and this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you about Sljivancanin. You said that "At that time, apart from Sljivancanin and Kuzmic I personally did not see any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other soldiers of the so-called JNA or Chetniks inside the hospital at the time. I mean, those three days, until the 20th."

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, in the morning, Sljivancanin appeared yet again -- Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking you about these three days.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Those three days? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Please look at this statement that you gave. And I received this as a document along with your statement. This is what you told the investigating judge, Zvonko Kuharic. "On the 13th of December, 1993 --"

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Is this an official note?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, it's not the official note. I'll give it to you straight away for you to have a look at it as soon as I read what you said happened on the 18th of November. This is what you said here: "That night, from the yard, gunfire could be heard, small arms gunfire, and Duvnjak Stanko and Mandic Marko were killed then because they fell into the hands of the Chetniks. At any rate, during that night I noticed that the Chetniks had different uniforms, those that were locally made and those that were foreign made. From time to time, they would barge into the hospital, and that's where there were patients mostly and those civilians who had sought shelter there. Whoever they recognised, they took out and there's been no trace of these people." So this was on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: That's when the hospital fell. When Mr. Sljivancanin took Marin Vidic, that's when this happened, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that nobody entered the hospital for three days, and this happened on the 18th of November, and that's what you described. Please take a look at this.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I got a bit confused, but I'm telling you the truth now. This happened at the moment when Mr. Sljivancanin went out with Marin Vidic. That's when the hospital fell. That's when the hospital fell. Do you understand what I'm saying? It was on the 17th or the 18th -- it was between the 18th and the 19th, at midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say the Chetniks barged in?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no JNA there.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Kuzmic was in the JNA. He came there and he talked to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, please, not then. Those three days.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I really have no idea what I should say to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this statement can be exhibited. Perhaps the Court would require this statement. It's for you to judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got a huge amount of material.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me something in relation to the hospital. In the hospital you met Batarelo Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, what I'm telling you now --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: He was killed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm using this information on the basis of the statement that you gave that I got from the OTP. When you were in hospital, did Mr. Batarelo Zeljko tell you that he --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That he had tried to penetrate the railroad across the bridge but they couldn't get there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Krsic Slavko [phoen] was killed there and Simo Bandelin [phoen]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And Batarelo got into a ditch?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where he spent the night and then he came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: He was not wounded.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So he sought shelter there at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: We were there together for one night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how many more people were in the hospital who had not been wounded at all and who had taken part in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: What a strange question. I mean, people who took part in the fighting and who had not been wounded. Well, those people who were in the hospital did not take part in the fighting at all except for the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there people like Batarelo who did take part in this penetration and then he sought shelter in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: I also wanted to be part of this penetration, breaking-up, because we all wanted to save ourselves. We didn't want to meet the military or paramilitaries in Vukovar because we knew what awaited us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is my last question: Before you said that in hospital there were people who were members of the ZNG and who had not been wounded --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC
utterances.text: Who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no redirect. There is one matter that I wanted to bring to the Court's attention that came up in proofing. I don't know that it's appropriate to discuss that in front of the witness. If -- if perhaps the Court has no questions, if the witness could withdraw but remain available to answer any questions if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We've got one document, the registrar reminds me. Mr. Milosevic, it's one of your documents. It's dated the 18th of September, 1991. The witness did recognise it. Do you want it exhibited, this one, 18th of September? It was an order of some sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll give it the next D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 167, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. It's pointed out it was the 8th of September, not the 18th. Mr. Cakalic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I kindly ask the Honourable Presiding Judge something, please, by your leave? Just two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not normal, quite honestly, but we'll see. If you want to raise something very briefly, you can raise it. We'll see what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say this now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I have a request. I have a request. I have something to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid -- I'm afraid not. We can't allow you to ask him questions here. But thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to bring to the Court's attention that during proofing we did show the witness a series of photographs, and this is because he said that Colonel Mrksic, he identified him as being at Ovcara. Amongst the photographs we showed him were photographs of Mrksic, and he was not able to identify him as the colonel or as somebody that he had seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You make that as a formal admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And that will be noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness, I understand, has protective measures and we'll need to take the precautions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are we likely to finish his evidence today? It seems unlikely, given the time estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think not, Your Honour. I would hope to finish the examination in chief and then hopefully there will be time for his cross-examination to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He'll be back next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I've already discussed that with the witness and he's available at the Court's convenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might raise a matter while we're waiting for the witness. There are a series of documents that we will use with the witness. They are his personnel records, and we will be asking that they be tendered under seal. It will be far more expeditious if we are able to use the Sanction system, but that would require the amici not to have their monitors turned on to the Sanction system but simply to use the binders that they've been provided. If they're willing to do that, I think it would be the better way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I could ask that two exhibit numbers -- well, the registrar is not here, so I'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Groome, when the witness is ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just while we're waiting, if I could ask that two exhibit numbers be assigned. One is a binder of 12 tabs of exhibits, and the other is a binder with one exhibit that I'll be just asking be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 505 for the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be convenient to deal with the other one when we get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal simply with the binder at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, pursuant to an order of the court to protect your identity, I will refer to you as B-127 during the course of your evidence here today. I would ask that we begin your testimony by asking that you be shown Prosecution Exhibit 505, tab 1. And my question to you is: Is that your name printed at the top of the very first line of that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes, that's my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does that document accurately record your educational and professional background? The witness is indicating he was not able to hear my question. I'll repeat it: Does that Prosecution Exhibit 505, tab 1, accurately reflect your educational and professional background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a few more biographical questions I would seek to ask. I'd ask that we go into private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, in Prosecution Exhibit 505, tab 1, you describe your ethnic background as being Yugoslav. Do you characterise yourself as being a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: I still declare myself that way. It has to do with the following: From the 6th of April, 1992, I always felt that I was a Yugoslav officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, others who might seek to classify you into one of the three groups, either Croat, Muslim, or Serb, how would they classify you? If they wanted to put you into one of those ethnicities, what would you be considered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In terms of ethnicity, in that form, others classified me as a Muslim. When I say "Muslim," I'm not referring to religious affiliation, I am talking about belonging to a nation, to an ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the spring of 1992. Were you stationed in Banja Luka during that time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you present during the takeover of Banja Luka by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes. I was there throughout this period of time, and I was a witness to everything that happened. From 1990, my place of residence was Banja Luka, so I was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to characterise for the Chamber the level of fighting that occurred between different sides or different factions during the takeover of Banja Luka in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, there was some street fighting -- or rather, there was not any street fighting or any such activity. It has to do with the following: The Serb defence forces -- or to be -- to put it in our language, the SOS took over Banja Luka. And since then, it's been under Serb authority. It has to do with the following: There wasn't any fighting. These units simply took over, both the key facilities in town, the municipality, the bridges, the entrances into town. During those days, Banja Luka was sealed off. But if we are to talk about fighting, there wasn't any to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to give -- describe in a little greater detail what you know about this SOS. Were they paramilitaries, police? Can you give a few more details about that group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: At that time, in 1992, that is to say, March/April 1992, these units were established from the reservists who were in the theatre of war in Eastern Slavonia and throughout Croatia and had returned to Banja Luka. At that point in time, they were considered to be paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe how the non-Serb population of Banja Luka was treated after this SOS group took over the town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: As for the non-Serb population, suffice it to say that it is a fact that when the SOS took over, the representatives of other parliamentary members did not have access to the city assembly. As for ordinary people, there is nothing worth mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you referred to other parliamentary members, are you talking elected representatives that were of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Correct. These are delegates, MPs, non-Serbs who were elected in the legal and legitimate elections in 1991 in the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when non-Serbs in Banja Luka began to lose their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: From then onwards, all employed persons who were non-Serbs lost their jobs. They were quite simply dismissed or they were told not to come to work at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the time that the SOS paramilitaries took over the town and the non-Serbs were being fired from their jobs, can you give the Chamber some sense of the level of JNA presence in the town during that time period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In that period of time, the Yugoslav People's Army was present with all its units, and there weren't any clashes between the SOS units and the army units. Later on, agreement was reached concerning the fact that there was one single objective involved and that practically the town was in Serb hands and that it wasn't necessary to have any major security forces in the streets of Banja Luka. Rather, activities should be geared towards the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate for the Chamber the approximate number of JNA troops that were actually present in Banja Luka during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: All the units were present there. However, a fact should be mentioned in this respect, and that is that this is a period of time when non-Serbs in the ranks of the Yugoslav People's Army were leaving the army and had left it altogether. As for the Yugoslav People's Army at that point in time, it was practically a Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a paramilitary group that referred to themselves as the Wolves from Vucjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with them, and I did have some contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have conversations with members of that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes. This happened in 1991, in the month of November, during the capture of the TV transmitter of TV Sarajevo in those days and turning around that same transmitter to broadcast the signals of Radio Television Serbia. Or rather, in those days it was Belgrade Radio Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did members of that unit indicate to you where they had been for their training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to them in an office as they had asked us to assist them in food, quartermaster supplies. And during those conversations, they told us that they had completed training in Knin and that actually they had been trained by Captain Dragan over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did some of the members of this unit wear a distinctive piece of head gear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: They were men which had non-establishment weapons, and they were not clothed in a uniform manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe their uniform or what they wore as best as you can recall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In those days, they wore camouflage uniforms which were still not widespread among members of the JNA in those days, and these were different kinds of uniforms but mostly camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniform in as much detail as you can, including any head gear that they wore.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Each one of them wore a red beret, camouflage uniforms that were olive-green grey, which up until then were not present within our units, and the beret was either on their heads or at their belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the person by the name of Captain Pavic from this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: The then-company commander was Pavic. He had contact with them, and in those days those men who had come to take control of the transmitters of TV Sarajevo were considered a danger for the unit, and so he undertook certain steps to protect the unit, so that he informed General Uzelac about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he make a request of General Uzelac regarding this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: The request was that in view of the fact that these men were considered to be paramilitaries, the request was for those men to leave the transmitter area; otherwise, General Uzelac would ask for aid from Zeljevo [phoen] airport for two MiG planes to come and destroy the transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did they respond to that threat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: After that, they picked up their equipment and left the transmitter of TV Sarajevo. But after that, the TV Sarajevo transmitter continued to broadcast the signal of Television Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now turn your attention to mosques in the Banja Luka municipality. Were you present during the destruction of a large number of those mosques?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes, I was present there. In those days I performed the duties of the man on duty in the Vrbas Barracks. I'm referring to the month of May. Between the 7th and the 8th of May, 1992, I was on duty and I was a witness of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During that time period, was there any fighting in and around Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: I wish first of all to make a correction. I may have said 1992, but I really meant 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The correction is noted. Was there any fighting during that time period, of 1993 -- May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In that period, in the town of Banja Luka there was no fighting whatsoever. I was on duty at the Vrbas Barracks, and if there had been any fighting, I would have known it, either from the person who was on duty in the garrison or -- and there were no events that would resemble any kind of combat activity or herald any combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you witness that night that -- what did you witness that night in connection with the destruction of mosques?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In view of the location of the Vrbas Barracks, I couldn't see anything, but I could hear, around 3.00 a.m,. two very powerful explosions in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, prior to this day, if there had been emergencies in the town, were you able to hear from the barracks the sounds of fire department sirens, and police sirens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: I didn't hear any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you ordinarily have been able to hear sirens of those two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. departments in the event of other emergencies in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Of course. One would have heard if there was any large-scale activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next day or the morning of the same day, did you go to visit the sites from where you heard the explosions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: After I handed over duty, I headed home. And on the way home, as I walked, I saw that the Ferhadija mosque had been destroyed and bulldozers had already arrived to clear up the rubble. Around the mosque, there was a lot of broken glass, and the police of the Banja Luka MUP was providing security around the destroyed mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was -- were the sites of some of the destroyed mosques turned into other uses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: The place where the Ferhadija mosque used to stand was subsequently covered with concrete, the area was cleared, and all that remained was the ancillary building of the mosque, and I think it's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you present in Banja Luka when a Catholic church was destroyed in a similar fashion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In 1995, after the fall of Eastern Slavonia, what happened was that the Catholic church was destroyed as a kind of revanchism in retaliation, in fact, for the fall of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to a person commonly known as Arkan. Did there come a time when members of your unit were deployed in the same area where Arkan's men was operating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In addition to the basic tasks the unit had, our unit was also occasionally assigned additional tasks on the frontline. I'm referring to infantry assignments. And we engaged in these as assistance on the frontline. In 1995, this unit was in the region of Drvar, where it had been assigned to secure that part of the frontline, and certain events happened which involved, among other things, the wounding of an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska, and there was some looting, looting of Serb houses by Arkan's men. Serb houses among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You spoke about the wounding of an officer. Were Arkan's men implicated in the wounding of that VRS officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: That man was performing his duty as he was ordered to do. He was on duty for 15 days on the frontline. That was his shift. And when he was due to go home because the regular replacement had arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: -- he was caught --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. The particular circumstances aren't as important as whether or not Arkan was implicated or Arkan's men were implicated in the wounding of that officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a response from the VRS command with respect to the wounding of this officer? And if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: The reaction was as follows: After a report as to what was going on over there, General Ninkovic sent a report to General Mladic, and General Mladic actually ordered Arkan's men to be kicked out. And after that, he was no longer in the region. As far as I know, he reappeared in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I can draw your attention to the period of time when the JNA officially withdrew from Bosnia and the Army of Republika Srpska or VRS was formed. Were you present in Banja Luka during that time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: I was in Banja Luka throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to describe in a -- on a theoretical level how the names of units were changed. I will ask to go into private session for you to tell us the specific change that was made to your unit. So can you tell us just generally, were the names of the JNA units altered? And if so, how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: As far as changes in the numerical name of the unit is concerned, they did happen, and the unit, for instance, that withdrew from Croatia was given a certain number in front of its basic number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go into private session briefly for you -- for the witness to describe his particular unit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I would now like to ask you to deal with the topic of what happened to the equipment of the former JNA as it withdrew from Slovenia, Croatia, and then eventually Bosnia. Can you describe in general terms what happened to that equipment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In concrete terms, the equipment of the former Yugoslav People's Army in units that were located within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia -- for example, MiG 29 planes flew to Batajnica and some other resources, but in that period quite a lot of the equipment that belonged to the unit remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was that equipment evenly distributed among the Bosnian government and the Republika Srpska government, or can you describe in greater detail who it was left to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: We are talking about the period of the spring of 1992, when the Muslims and Croats had already abandoned the ranks of the units of the JNA, and that equipment belonged only to the Army of Republika Srpska that was formed in those days. There's no question of any distribution. Any reference along those lines is not serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When the JNA withdrew from Slovenia, did you become aware of air navigation equipment that was removed from Cerklje [phoen] air force base in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: That's not the right name. We are talking about the Crklje airport that was located in Slovenia, and a mixed air brigade that was situated in Slovenia was dislocated to Mahovljani airport near Banja Luka. However, that brigade was called 92, and the number 8 was added in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has heard some evidence about a no-fly zone and its establishment. Can I ask you to describe the geographical area that was the subject of the no-fly zone in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: With the introduction of the no-fly zone, depending on the time we're talking about, flights could be carried out only with special permission from UN command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what area was subjected to this no-fly zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: The area covered the entire territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based upon your duties and the information that you had access to officially, were you aware of violations of this no-fly zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Violations of the no-fly zone did occur, and it was sometimes necessary to do so, and it happened mostly in the edges, that is, the area of the Ponikve Crklje airport, an airport located near Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 505, tab 4. There are actually two documents in this tab, Your Honour. The Prosecution is withdrawing the second of these documents, which end in ERN number 5868, and is asking that the witness be shown the single document which remains ending in ERN 4149.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to take a look at this document. And if you're able, can you describe what is contained in this document. Sir, I'm going to draw your attention to a particular portion of that document on the television screen in front of you. You have the entire document there to place it in context. Can you summarise just in general terms what that document is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: First of all, this document basically consists of instructions for command and coordinated action in PVO and air support. It was compiled by the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, approved by General Ratko Mladic. And in that document, this part has to do with coordinated action by PVO and air support from Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Army of Yugoslavia. The aim was to define the separation belt, exchange of information on the situation in the air space, exchange of officers for coordinated action at command posts, exchange of announcement of flights, and preparation of joint plans on the use of forces, and the preparation of the coordinated action plan, that is, with the command of -- in Yugoslavia and the air forces in the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now draw your attention to a particular part of that document on the television screen before you and ask for your comment on that particular portion. And that is paragraph 3 of the document -- or section 3. And if you would, would you explain the significance of this order with respect to the no-fly zone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: This document prescribes all activities -- could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please place this order into the context of the no-fly zone. What -- what relationship does it have or what relevance does it have to the imposition of a no-fly zone over Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: These are instructions for the activities of units prescribed on the basis of the situation that has set in and with the introduction of the no-fly zone for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If these instructions are followed, would it permit violations of the no-fly zone to go undetected by international peacekeepers and observers present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Every army seeks to conceal its traces, violations of certain rules which had been prescribed at that point in time. In one of the orders, in fact, and instructions, it is said how this should be done if such flights were to be discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that a convenient place to take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have a request from the registry for you to clarify what document you are withdrawing. We, in fact, have only one document, I think, in this tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies. It was withdrawn this morning before it was actually handed up to the Chamber. I was unaware that it had been already done, so my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To just make sure I've got the right tab number, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's tab 4, Your Honour. And the ERN number at the top right-hand corner of the page should read 03014149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that clarifies it. We'll adjourn now. Witness B-127, could you remember in this adjournment and any others not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. If you would be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, there seems to have been some addition to the witness's screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is advised. It's a low-tech solution to the problem of glare, to make it possible for the witness to -- to see the TV screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems a fairly -- a fairly Heath Robinson. It's cardboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is. Luckily we have face distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if I could now draw your attention to a different topic. Can I ask you to describe from your perspective the changes in personnel in the Army of the VRS as the JNA formally withdrew from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: With the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army, or rather, when it lost its name the Yugoslav People's Army, a transformation of the army took place, of the army that was in the area. And this was what happened: The officers who remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina and belonged to the former JNA just became members of the Army of Yugoslavia through the 30th Personnel Centre. The people who were doing their service - I'm talking about the Serbs who were serving in Serbia and Montenegro - were transferred to Bosnia and that's where they received their assignments. A certain number of commanding officers who were born in Serbia were withdrawn from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically from Banja Luka too, and flights -- air force flights were organised, taking them back -- air lifts back to Serbia. The officers who were in Bosnia-Herzegovina became officers of the Army of Yugoslavia, as I say, through the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after the -- after the JNA formally withdrew from Bosnia, were you ever present when a number of VJ, Yugoslav army, reservists came to the Banja Luka area to conduct operations or to be involved in operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In 1992, in the autumn, I was in the Vrbas barracks when three busloads with Valjevo number plates arrived. They arrived at the barracks to spend the night there and continue their way the next morning to the front. They were given accommodation for the night, dinner and breakfast, and they left in the morning, taking the direction of Bihac. I talked to one of these men, and one of them told me that he had been mobilised in Bubanj -- to Bubanj Potok, in fact, which is in Belgrade. And I asked him man to man, "Did you have to come?" And he said, "I would have lost my job had I refused to respond to the call-up for mobilisation."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how many men were involved in this deployment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Approximately 180 men. There were -- all the busses were full, and each bus carried about 45 to 48 people, 45 to 48 seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want now -- I want to now ask you about any changes to the communications systems as you have -- of which you have personal knowledge. Before we do that, it will be necessary for us to -- or for you to describe in greater detail your specific command and its relationship to other commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that we go into private session for this purpose, and ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 505, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, before I ask you specific questions about the data link you've referred to, I want to ask you some questions just generally about how the radar system operated in the former Yugoslavia. And my first question to you is: Would it be fair to say that a radar operator, looking at a screen of the air space of the former Yugoslavia, was receiving information that was collected by a number of individual radar antennas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because all the information and the targets discovered in the air space were identified and processed, this whole air space was analysed, and data processed in this way was then sent on to the commands and other users, beneficiaries, the missile units, the centres for alarming the population and reporting, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, prior to 1991, did -- was there a unified centralised air defence system for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: In the territory of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there was a joint system for controlling the air space, and it was a unified system with continuous surveillance of the air space, which meant 24-hour supervision and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened to this unified system after the JNA withdrew from Slovenia and then the JNA withdrew from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: With the withdrawal of the units, both from Slovenia and from Croatia, and the units which belonged to the 5th Regiment of air surveillance, they had to be dislocated, moved, and so the regiment from Zagreb was relocated to Bihac when the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they withdrew from Bihac, and the battalion withdrew to Banja Luka. As far as the links are concerned, the newly arisen situation had to be catered to so that new channels of communication were open with the regiment's relocation to Bihac and Belgrade. And when I mean withdrawing them to Belgrade, I mean the RViPV command through the radio relay communication links. And so when the battalion was relocated from Bihac to Banja Luka, new -- from the document that we were looking at a moment ago, there was cooperation. They acted jointly, in fact. And the ViPVO centre then became linked with the radar positions at Banovci and the ViPV commands, so that they were able to see what we saw in the air space, surveying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can rephrase that in layman's terms, and if you would affirm or correct where I've gone wrong. So the information, from what you're saying, is after the JNA withdrew from Bosnia it maintained the data link which allowed the VRS air defence system to see what the radar antennas in Serbia and Montenegro were picking up, and vice versa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Those links were established when the battalion moved from Bihac to Banja Luka. New data links were opened, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did the information shared -- was it as I described it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes. Radio relay links were established, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've used a few abbreviations. Can I ask you to describe in greater detail what the abbreviations mean. You've used the abbreviation RViPVO. Can you describe what that signifies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: The abbreviation RViPVO means air force and anti-air defence, or rather, air defence. In the Army of Republika Srpska, what was used was ViPVO, the air force and PVO, air force and air defence. So when we're talking about ViPVO, this was part of the Army of Republika Srpska and RViPVO referred to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this data link, what is the latest period in time that you are able to say from your personal knowledge that data link existed allowing VRS air defence personnel to see what was coming from the radar antennas in Serbia and Montenegro? What's the latest point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: The last moment, latest period, was the introduction of IFOR, IFOR's prohibition of the radar and computer devices, because the radar -- and the radar stopped working then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, when was that? What was the month and year of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Straight after the war. We're talking about 1996, 1997. And after that, permission was given for the radar and computer devices for pure maintenance, for their maintenance, a certain number of hours were allocated. So no combat operations of those units existed any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just incidentally, prior to the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, did the JNA have any similar relationship with a neighbouring country, whereby it permitted the automatic transfer of its data from its radar stations to go to other countries such as Hungary or other countries it perceived to be friendly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: As far as those data are concerned, they were just used for our own country, and there was a certain number for civil aviation was permitted with respect to an exchange of information when civil aviation, or rather, civilian airplanes flew from one country to another, they could access that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how about with respect to military aircraft?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Only for our own users. There was absolutely no way in which we would inform Hungary or Romania, for example. It was only for the needs of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony you referred a number of times to the 30th Personnel Centre. Can I ask you to describe what your understanding is of the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: The 30th Personnel Centre of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia was a department in the personnel administration of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. It was established at that point in time when the war in Bosnia began, or at least I didn't know about it up until then. But when the war began, I received papers where it said as a heading "The 30th Personnel Centre." And the markings for that 30th Personnel Centre was military post 3001, VP 3001.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say the -- the markings were military post 3001, are you saying that that's the number that was used to indicate that a document had originated from the 30th Personnel Centre? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And the document came from the 30th Personnel Centre if it had the stamp of the 30th Personnel Centre on it with the VP 3001 code on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm going to work with the witness and put to the witness a number of personnel records, beginning with his own. I have kept the records for each individual in the same tab as I believed that would be the way to avoid confusion. I hope it works out that way. The particular documents that I will refer to have been indicated with coloured tabs. I will refer to those tabs and also the last few digits of the ERN and ask the Chamber to advise me if it is becoming confusing, and I will try to -- to deal with it as clearly as possible. The first set of exhibits I'm going to ask the witness to deal with, and we will attempt to do this on the Sanction system. It will be the first document in the tab of the binder that Your Honours have. And I would ask the director, this next series of documents in tab 5, I'd ask that none of these be broadcast, as they would reveal the identify of this witness. And if the amici could switch off their Sanction computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the document that we can see on the screen now - it ends in ERN number 2876 - what is this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Would you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarise what the document is that we're looking at on the screen. I believe you have a hard copy of it in your hand at the moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: This is a medical card or ID of which I am the owner. You can see who my commander was. It states when I began working first and when I received medical insurance from the army first. You can see my name and surname and the place of residence. On the second page, where it says "PS1" are stamps indicating that I am insured, I have health insurance and military insurance by the 30th Personnel Centre, VP 3001 Belgrade, the military post code.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the address that's indicated here, it's an address in Bosnia; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're in open session, so there's no need to go into specific detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that that specific street reference be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the address that's indicated here, is this military property that you are -- you had the right to stay in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: It was a military institution and a military hotel, an army hotel, in fact, which accommodated officers of the former JNA and later to become the Army of Republika Srpska, including civilians too -- or rather, workers employed in the army, who were in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the -- the second page that you've referred to, it bears a number of stamps and it has a number of endorsements. Are these markings intended to indicate that you are still an active member of the 30th Personnel Centre and entitled to certain medical benefits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And it states here that it is the military post 3001 Belgrade, and that I received health insurance from that military post.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So two of these endorsements are from the 30th Personnel Centre in Belgrade, and two of them are from Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. They were certified both in Banja Luka and in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you required to maintain similar medical cards for members of your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127
